topics.title: Review and solution reasoning
topics.summary: Why does assignment through a reference not reseat it? The reference remains bound to its original target; assignment changes that target’s value according to the target type’s operation.

cards.question: Why does assignment through a reference not reseat it?
cards.answer: The reference remains bound to its original target; assignment changes that target’s value according to the target type’s operation.

cards.question: Why can const reference still observe a changing object?
cards.answer: Constness restricts that access path. Other permitted aliases may affect the underlying state, so broader immutability requires a broader design.

cards.question: Why test a failure at the last element?
cards.answer: It reveals whether earlier elements were modified before the operation discovered the rejection condition.

cards.question: Why keep element references short-lived?
cards.answer: Fewer intervening operations can invalidate the target, making the lifetime argument easier to inspect.

cards.question: What does int& alias = value; create?
cards.answer: It creates a reference bound to value. The two names refer to the same int object; it does not create a second independent int.

cards.question: Can assignment reseat an existing reference?
cards.answer: No. alias = other assigns to the object alias already refers to. It does not make alias refer to other instead.

cards.question: Why must an ordinary reference be initialized?
cards.answer: It needs a target when it is created. A declaration such as int& r; cannot leave it waiting to be bound later.

cards.question: What does const std::vector<int>& promise at this access path?
cards.answer: The function borrows the vector and cannot mutate it through that reference. Other allowed access paths may still exist; const is not a global freeze.

cards.question: Why use a value parameter for a small input like int delta?
cards.answer: It is cheap to copy and makes an independent input. A reference is useful only when borrowing or caller-state mutation is part of the contract.

cards.question: What does auto& change in a range-based loop?
cards.answer: It binds the loop variable to each actual element. Changes through it affect the collection; auto alone would create a separate value.

cards.question: Why can a returned reference be unsafe even if the type is correct?
cards.answer: Its target may already be dead or become invalidated. Type checking does not by itself prove that the caller's later use occurs within the target's lifetime.

cards.question: What is aliasing in a function call?
cards.answer: Two parameters or names can refer to the same underlying object. A design must account for that when writes affect later reads.

cards.question: Why validate a whole batch before modifying its first element?
cards.answer: Otherwise a late invalid element can leave earlier elements changed. Validate first or use a candidate copy when rejection must preserve the original collection.

cards.question: Does a const reference always avoid all lifetime concerns?
cards.answer: No. It still borrows an object. The binding context determines any temporary lifetime extension; returning a reference to expired data remains unsafe.

cards.question: How can the caller understand whether a helper mutates input?
cards.answer: A non-const reference signals possible mutation, but a clear name and documented contract explain when changes happen and what failure preserves.

cards.question: What must stay true while a function borrows a collection?
cards.answer: The collection and referenced elements must remain alive, and operations must not invalidate borrowers that are still used. The borrow does not own them.

cards.question: What must bool shiftAll(std::vector<int>& values, int delta) accept and reject?
cards.answer: Input elements and delta are -100 through 100. Shift every value by delta only if every result stays in -100 through 100. Otherwise return false with the whole vector unchanged.
